How does Git help trace changes to a SQL database project?
column2:
Commits record the project's version history.
Review a commit's diff to see which object definitions changed.
Review source

column1: Why keep one database object's definition in each source file?
column2:
It makes object-level changes easier to review in Git diffs.
A table change and a procedure change appear in their respective files.
Review source

column1: What is a common folder organization for SQL project schema files?
column2:
Group files by object type, such as Tables, Views, and StoredProcedures.
Use consistent names so that developers can locate related definitions.
Review source

column1: Why exclude generated .dacpac build outputs from the source repository?
column2:
The build recreates them from the versioned project source.
Store pipeline artifacts separately rather than mixing generated output with source files.
Review source

column1: What is reference data in a database deployment?
column2:
Application lookup values, such as status codes or region lists.
These controlled values support application behavior rather than recording individual business transactions.
Review source

column1: Why version reference data scripts alongside the database schema?
column2:
To deploy required lookup values consistently with the schema that uses them.
Schema definitions alone do not populate lookup rows.
Review source

column1: When does a pre-deployment script execute?
column2:
Before the generated deployment plan executes.
Use it for preparation that must precede the planned schema changes.
Review source

column1: Which deployment script normally populates lookup tables after their schema changes?
column2:
The post-deployment script.
It runs after the deployment plan, so newly created tables are available.
Review source

column1: How many pre-deployment and post-deployment entry scripts can one SQL project declare?
column2:
At most one of each.
Each optional entry script can include multiple files using SQLCMD directives.
Review source

column1: When is the deployment plan calculated relative to the pre-deployment script?
column2:
Before the pre-deployment script executes.
Do not assume that schema changes inside that script automatically cause the plan to be recalculated.
Review source

column1: Why exclude SQLCMD-included seed files from database-model compilation?
column2:
They contain deployment-time data statements rather than declarative schema definitions.
The build still combines their contents into the packaged deployment script.
Review source

column1: How can you inspect the combined deployment scripts inside a built .dacpac?
column2:
Open a copy as a ZIP archive and inspect the packaged .sql scripts.
The build combines included files into one script for each deployment-script type.
Review source

column1: What makes a reference data script idempotent?
column2:
Rerunning it preserves the intended data state without introducing duplicate rows.
Match existing keys and update or insert as needed instead of blindly repeating INSERT statements.
Review source

column1: What happens when multiple MERGE source rows match one target row for UPDATE?
column2:
SQL Server raises an error.
Keep the seed source unique on its matching key.
Review source

column1: Why does an idempotent MERGE still need concurrency testing?
column2:
Concurrent executions can race or conflict when inserting or updating keys.
Safe repeated execution does not guarantee safe simultaneous execution.
Review source

column1: What happens to target-only rows when MERGE has no WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clause?
column2:
That MERGE specifies no action for those rows.
An update-and-insert seed script does not automatically delete target rows omitted from its source list.
Review source
